Hiby RS2 II Review
​
"The True Darwin Evolution of a Pure Audio Player"

By: 
Chris Love
​
Hiby RS2 II Review 
​
Intro
​
Hello, this review and feature covers the latest digital audio player from the audio brand 
Hiby
, named the Hiby 
RS2 II ($439)
. I should have said the “highly anticipated” successor to one of the more beloved non-Android daps. That beloved dap is of course the 
Hiby RS2
. The OG R2R dap that almost started a movement away from Android based digital audio players. I for one never had the opportunity to review the OG RS2 and I only had a couple days to listen to it, but I can tell you that I was very impressed with it. Once I found out that Hiby was coming out with a newer version, I had to check it out. Of course, I am still awaiting the RS2 II to arrive as it’s currently enroute to my home and should be here in a few days. I was told that patience is a virtue, but it’s very difficult to have patience waiting for this highly anticipated (by me) device to come along. Nevertheless, this gives me time to brush up on this device and try to learn as much as I can about it. I can see from marketing material that Hiby changed some things up, upgraded some components, kept what made the OG special, and added some size. Ya know, I always get on brands who create another version of their products without actually upgrading the newer version. Well, from what I can tell Hiby actually did “upgrade” the OG RS2 with this latest model. 
What is the RS2 II? 
​
So, you are seeking out a solid “under $500” dap and you see that Hiby is coming out with a brand new $439 dap of their own. Of course, I’m speaking of the RS2 II. One thing you may notice is that this thing has no wifi, no Bluetooth, no bells and whistles that are popular today. You can’t check your email on it, watch a video, play a game or stream Qobuz, Tidal, or any other music streaming service available nowadays. That doesn’t mean that it doesn’t have bells and whistles, it just means that the RS2 II’s features are all music related, audio related, and sonically prioritized. I would say that the major selling point of this dap is exactly that. That is, the RS2 II is profoundly geared towards listening to music in its purest digital form… for the cost. I have to be truthful with you all, I adore daps whose sole focus is music. I have quite a few of them and they always get play time. Don’t get me wrong, my favorite daps do have Android attached, however I am very curious if the RS2 II can upend the hierarchy of my dap collection. I’ve never owned a non-Android dap with an internal architecture such as the RS2 II has. You see, the other major selling point of the Hiby RS2 II is that it is what’s known as an “R2R” dap. However, it isn’t just that it’s R2R, but it is highly intriguing that this R2R dap is utilized within Hiby’s own Darwin III. Their 3rd generation digital audio processing and digital to analogue conversion system which comes with an R2R resistor ladder dac. It’s basically Hiby’s fully functional processing and conversion platform, for lack of better words. In truth, I’m only scratching the surface and I’m writing purely out of gleeful childlike expectancy and impatience. This is one device that I know (even before I hear it) that I’m going to review it. 
Hiby
​
What can I say that I haven’t already said about this brand? Hiby has been around since (I believe) 2011 and has been a huge player in the personal audio game for many of those years. I actually found out that Hiby didn’t start out as a hardware-first company. Hiby actually broke bread with the hobby in the software side developing different operating systems and music player software. However, today you can find the name “Hiby” attached to a broad and very diverse range of products as well as one of the most successful and loved Android and Linux based music player apps named the 
Hiby Music Player
. Beyond the software stuff I really feel that Hiby has made their name on their daps. Granted, they’ve crafted and created some very high quality and well-tuned iems as well as even wireless products and of course, they’ve absolutely nailed the dongle dac side of the business. However, in my opinion it is in digital audio players that Hiby has truly stood out. Friends, they have brought to market some of the most beloved and popular daps in every price category, and each has always been right at the forefront of the audio landscape for tech, innovation, and knowing what hobbyists desire to see in their daps. I know because I’ve personally owned many of them and even reviewed a handful too. 
Reviews
​
Personally, I know that if a product comes with the name Hiby attached, that it’ll be a solid product. There are plenty of brands that I feel this way about. Brands like Shanling, Fiio, Simgot, Letshuoer, and many more. That said, for me, Hiby is almost set apart from the rest. I’ve actually reviewed a handful of Hiby products, and each provided me with great enjoyment as each is highly competitive against the market in respect to their price range and type. Products like the flat-out stellar 
Hiby Zeta
 which proved to the audio world that Hiby could create a kilo-buck flagship that could contend with any kilo-buck set in its range. Another extremely well-crafted product is the wonderful 
Hiby R6 Pro II
, which I featured a couple years ago, and I am still recommending it. Next, the unsung and beautifully tuned 
Hiby Yvain
 which has one of the better all-BA midrange performances that you’ll hear. I also loved the 
Hiby R3 II
. The tiny non-Android dap that I was fortunate to review. I even reviewed a very unique product which is part of Hiby’s sister brand Hiby Digital named the 
Hiby Digital Xeno
. A MEMs driver set that truly surprised me. Next was one of my favorite single DD iems under $150, the 
Hiby Yacht 10
. My advice; check that set out. After that I featured debatably my favorite non-Android dap under $250 in the 
Hiby R3 Pro II
. My word does the R3 Pro II sound good! Then came the wonderful 
Hiby R6 Pro II 2025
 (follow-up from the OG R6 Pro II). This dap has it all, a complete product, so well manufactured, designed, UI is fantastic, it’s fast, and so nice looking. Yet, best of all it sounds better than almost any dap under $700. To round things out, the last product that I’ve reviewed was the 
Hiby W4
. Once again, an awesome Bluetooth dac/amp that I use regularly since I got it. The point is that if the name Hiby is attached, it’ll very likely be a solid product. 
Well Hello Beautiful! 
​

The Hiby RS2 II arrived at my home and right away it was everything that I expected and anticipated it would be. Honeymoon phase in full force. The point where I’m not looking for any issues. Anyway, I quickly brushed through the UI, checked some settings, everything was smooth and it’s very apparent that the new dual-core processor is doing its job. Next, I moved right into the “I want to hear it” phase. I’ve held off long enough. Thankfully the RS2 II came fully charged and ready to rock ‘n roll so I quickly inserted a 1tb micro-SD card into one of its two micro-SD card slots. This card is stuffed with around 900 gb of music/albums. It made me very happy that it took about 10 minutes or less to load them all. Now, I will save the majority of what I heard for my actual review further down the line, but I was instantly impressed. I was so impressed that I wanted to hurry onto social media to post some impressions. Thankfully, I held off. I don’t like doing honeymoon phase posts as they are always too forward in expressive praise and I always feel that I go too hard too soon. Just know this, for all of the compromises that exist from not using an Android dap, those were all washed away and non-existent when I actually heard the RS2 II. Hiby deserves some well-earned fist bumps. That all said, I’m ready to get this one going. So, without further ado, the Hiby RS2 II…

​
–

–

–

Packaging / Accessories 
​
Unboxing
​
I love a very well thought out unboxing experience. To see something different than what we are used to seeing is always a treat. If it’s a treat for me then I know it’ll be a treat for you. Believe me, I’m overly jaded by this point. But I digress, the Hiby RS2 II arrived at my home in a special fitted cardboard outer box for shipping purposes that is actually quite nice. I mean, it’s just a cardboard box, but anytime I see that… I can bet everything that’s in my pockets that the contents will be at least moderately lavish. The outer shipping box has the name “Hiby RS2 II” imprinted in the center as well as “Darwin III” on the bottom. Open the cardboard box and you’ll get your look at the RS2 II’s beautifully made walnut wood case/box. 
What’s Inside? 
​
First off, friends, this storage box is crafted handsomely, with very sturdy metal hinges, magnetic snap shut lid, as well as a very charmingly highlighted dark wood grain meandering around all sides of this gorgeous case. Friends, I am speaking for anyone who has unboxed this dap and saying out loud that “Hiby, you are a CLASS ACT!” only a brand that has some class uses a box like this for a dap. So perfect for dap storage after unboxing as it’s a very good size (6 ⅜” x 6 ⅜” x 2 ¾”) to hold the RS2 II as well as a few sets of iems and other accessories. Of course, in the center of the lid you’ll see a deeply engraved “Hiby RS2 II”. Under the name you’ll also see “High Resolution Music Player”, also engraved. This is where you open the box and you’ll feel the tug of the box lid, the sturdy feel of quality materials moving smoothly. Upon opening you’ll first see a wood layer with two holes for fingers to pick it out. Under the lid is a felt gray covering with “Darwin III” imposed in the center in golden lettering. Take out the wood layer and there you will see the delightful Hiby RS2 II sitting safely inside of felt-covered-foam cut-outs. Lift that layer out and there will be a manual, quick start guide etc. (basically some reading material). Next, underneath the guide is three tightly packaged smaller boxes. In one box you’ll find the USB-C to USB-C charging cable and USB-C to USB-A adapter. Next to that you’ll find the very nice leather protective case as well as an extra screen protector (it arrives with a screen protector installed). In the last box is a very nice fabric cladded USB-C to RCA coaxial cable. Overall, I find this accessory list to be quite bountiful for this cost. Hiby did a nice job of adding pertinent inclusions. Especially the screen protector and protective case. However, I didn’t gloat enough about that storage box. It really is impressive folks and looks like something you’d get from a dap that costs four times this price. No joke. 
Protective Case
​

One addition that I’m always crossing my fingers at receiving in any dap unboxing is a protective case. I was so thrilled to see one inside of the RS2 II’s packaging. What’s best is this case is actually a very well-made slip-on case. Made out of genuine Italian leather with the internal side cladded all the way around in a soft felt material. It slips on very easily but doesn’t come off as easily, which is a very good thing. All ports have reasonably wide cut-out sections so I can use each button, the wheel, or plug in cables without having any trouble. However, what’s best is that this case looks very nice. Now, you can purchase this case separately for 
$39 here
 and it can be bought in either the tan/brown leather color or a forest green colorway. I actually really like the tan/brown case, but the RS2 II that I have has a forest green colorway which may look better with a matching forest green case. I don’t know, I like them both. The point is that the case is a very nicely thought-out addition and proves that Hiby is thinking about the consumer when adding a case that is pretty pricey on its own. So, a very nice addition. 
Build / Aesthetic / Internals / Layout / UI
​
Build Quality
​
I am speaking right now about the RS2 II that I have. That is the “standard version”, but you can also get the fully brass version as well. However, both versions are extremely well put together and made of quality materials. The Standard version comes with a fully aluminum CNC machined chassis in a rectangular form measuring approximately 91.95 x 62.05 x 18.6 mm and comes in with a fairly lightweight 156 grams, or roughly ⅓ LB. I love the size folks as it’s a smaller device, yet it also has a nicely sized screen (3.55”) with thinner bezels that gives the user a reasonably good-sized portrait style look at the UI and album art etc. Fits perfectly in one hand and can be used with one hand if I want to. The RS2 II has a very modern vibe, sharper edges, clean cuts, and tailored beautifully. On the back is a gorgeous Houndstooth-pattern design with two Allen-key screws holding it on. As far as buttons, all of the action is on the right side as you’ll see a rotary volume wheel/power button at the top, and 3 rectangular buttons in a row on the side panel. Those controls are as such; the first button is “previous track” and holding down will rewind. The middle button is “play/pause”, and the 3rd button is “next track” and hold down for fast forward. Also on the right side is a sample rate indicator light. On the bottom you’ll see the type-c charging port on the left as well as two micro-SD card slots. The micro-SD card slots come with dummy cards to use for dust protection when not in use (another thoughtful addition by Hiby). Lastly, on the top of the RS2 II are the 4.4 balanced and 3.5 single ended ports on the left (both ports come with dummy jacks to protect from dust (Hiby is awesome) as well as an “FN” switch which is a “user-selectable” switch that you can decide what function you’d like to use it for. I believe it comes programmed for a key-lock function. I adore the size, the weight, the placement of buttons, the placement of the 4.4 and 3.5 ports on top, and I love the rotary volume wheel. Such a well-made device. 
Aesthetic / Design
​
One thing I would say about the RS2 II’s aesthetic and design appeal is that it has a very modern and sleek visual appeal. Maybe I would call it “modern-hifi-architectural” with a luxurious vibe. Every machined cut is perfect, honed to perfection. The build quality is obviously stellar for the price (as it should be). I love the feel of this dap in my hands with the case off. I just get this sense of a premium device with the cold aluminum, the sharper angles, the mature hi-fi angled cuts. Just so beautifully made. I also like the chose of the Houndstooth-patterned back panel with its repetitive design features. Such a well thought out colorway too. It’s almost understated, almost, yet not loud either, and not muted or repetitive like so many black or silver colorways that we see so often. The front is all business, clean lines, bright screen, sharp surrounding frame, while the back is stylish, rhythmic in feel, fashion-oriented, and a very decorative choice. Next, for whatever reason the volume wheel adds such a nice visual touch. It has a decorative element to its design that gives the RS2 II a premium classic hi-fi appearance, for lack of better words. Overall, I’d say clean architectural, modern and sophisticated with a splash of quiet luxury. Hiby… well done. 
​
Internals
​
Now we get to the heart of this beautiful player. If I were to start somewhere in describing what’s inside of this player, I’d probably say that it’s spilt into three distinct sections. One is the analog stage using four OPA1612 devices used for buffering, filtering, and voltage along with four OPA1622 amplifier devices supplying the output current. Next is the anticipated Darwin III architecture where Hiby lists a PH1P35MEG324 FPGA. Hiby states that the Darwin III engine supplies 35,000 logic units and 40 DSP units. It lets Hiby do their own audio-processing and conversion control to adjust FIR digital filters, Harmonic adjustments, oversampling (with 32x oversampling identified in the description), oversampling/non-oversampling operation, R2R modeling using resistor style parameters as well as DSD processing too. The beauty is that Darwin III adds programmable processing and corrections within the conversion hardware. Another main section is the R2R dac section (which I’ll cover later). The RS2 II’s R2R dac section uses precision resistor networks which are controlled by resistor networks controlled by switches. Left and right channel R2R networks which are followed by analogue filters. This is not some conventional ESS Sabre dac, or an AKM, or Cirrus Logic style dac chip functionality. This is instead Hiby’s own Darwin R2R. There’re also two dedicated oscillators internally providing the timing etc. Hiby also added in a 3,500 mAH battery and 3.8 V with a 5V/2A charging ability and temperature dependent charging adjustments (more on that later too). Obviously, there are many more internal components, and I did a terrible job explaining the components I listed above. However, 0.01% of you actually care, so I will be moving on. 
Ports, Buttons, & Functionality
​
I already briefly explained the button layout as well as the volume wheel, what they do, how they function too. However, I want to quickly run through how well they function as well as some of the ports and what their duties are. First off, the volume wheel is awesome. It’s everything one would want with a very tactile click of each volume step, perfectly timed and adjusted. Raised enough for my thumb to easily operate it, even with the case on. Next, the buttons are exactly as I like them, on the right side and both haptic and tactile in feel. Friends, I could be blindfolded and stuck in a pitch-black room, and I could operate these buttons with zero problems. They’re all very much intuitive. As I said, you have many options for usage with these ports (USB-C, 3.5, 4.4). Altogether they help the RS2 II function as either a standalone player, a dac/headphone amplifier for another source, also a source for another external amplifier, or even a digital transport for use with another dac. That is, two analogue line outputs, two headphone outputs, a USB digital output, as well as a coaxial digital output. Each one offers another way to use the RS2 II and each functions very well. I may list some of these in the “Features” section later with a more thorough explanation. For now, just know that Hiby gives us solid functionality through physical buttons and the volume wheel as well as many possible ways of listening using the onboard ports that Hiby thoughtfully added. 
UI / Hiby OS
​

This is another section that could also be a borderline “feature”. Of course, I’m speaking about the UI software experience on the Hiby RS2 II. I’ll say first that the RS2 II runs a PureAudio Hiby OS which is a 100% music dedicated operating system and is miles away from any Android dap UI. I have to say, the RS2 II is very smooth. Much smoother than I would have predicted. They actually went with a highly capable Ingenic X1600E SoC operating system, Linux based, it’s this processor that runs the Darwin III system, the R2R resistor networks. Hiby actually declares a total of 64 mB of RAM is LPDDR2 Ram is integrated within its processor package. So yes, scrolling is very smooth with no hiccups, no lag, and no odd moments of freezing (which I expected). I think that the actual functionality of scrolling has been one of the largest surprises for me. How nicely album art shows up when quickly scrolling down the Albums tab, Artists, or the All-Music tab etc. It simply works well, which is very nice to see from a Linux based dap. 
UI
​
Once you turn the RS2 II on (which takes about 10 seconds) you’ll arrive at the home screen. Here you’ll see six touchscreen tabs. There’s Music, Darwin Filters, MSEB settings, System Settings, Play Settings screen, as well as an About screen. I’ll start with settings because Hiby provides a lot of nice options here. This is where you program the “FN” switch (on the top of the RS2 II), select language, choose a theme color, font size, which USB working mode (auto, device, OTG). You can also choose which USB device mode (Audio or Storage) you’d like, USB current can be limited, USB dac feedback setting, you can adjust the clock, choose idle shutdown time, sleep shutdown, charge protection, choose whether the battery percentage is listed at the top, you can change the Short-Cut Menu, choose if volume works with screen off, Screen Saver settings, Firmware Updates, and Restore Factory Settings among many other settings that I don’t feel like naming. There’s actually so many options folks. Tapping the Music tab will bring up six other tabs like All Music, Local Files, Albums, Artists, Genres, and Album Artist. You can also access playlists as well on this screen. Of course, you also have Darwin settings back on the home page. Inside you have the ability to choose you Darwin Filter (I’ll explain later), check the NOS (Non-Oversampling) box, as well as change the Harmonic Controller from #0-255. At the Home Screen swiping down will bring up the Shortcut menu which offers many functions that can be changed. Lastly, I also want to tell you about the Play Settings that I me toned earlier. Inside you can access the full graphic equalizer as well as the full PEQ (Perimetric EQ). You can Update the Music Database, go into Music Update Mode, DSD Output Mode, DSD Gain Compensation, here you have Gapless playback, Max Volume, Volume Limiter, Fixed Power-On Volume, Crossfade, Replay Gain, Balance, and about 10 other settings that are there. It’s a very robust system for an PureAudio OS. Far more comprehensive than any other non-Android daps I’ve used.

Features
​
Darwin III R2R Conversion
​
I have to imagine that the #1 selling point about the Hiby RS2 II has to be that it comes with the Darwin III conversion and processing architecture inside of such a compact player. It certainly was the original RS2’s main headline feature and I don’t think anything has changed. Rather than using a conventional dac chip that we’ve seen a thousand times in the past (by the way, there’s nothing wrong with those chips) like AKM, ESS Sabre chips, Cirrus Logic, Burr Brown and many more, the RS2 II smoothly combines FPGA processing with a resistor network digital to analogue conversion. It really is an awesome feature and clearly a reason to purchase. You’ll agree when you hear it folks. Anyways, rather than simply offering a fixed conversion mode (as we are used to) what this Darwin III architecture does; it provides listeners or hobbyists several different ways to check out the RS2 II’s presentation. It actually brings to the table many different processing options like switching between oversampling & non-oversampling, many harmonic adjustments which Hiby discloses is basically like adjusting the 2nd harmonic. It has selectable digital filters, native DSD processing, as well as R2R network modeling or correction etc. Listen folks, you’ll definitely know when you hear a good R2R dac and to my ears the HIBY RS2 II’s number one feature is what we all came here for… playing music. 
Non-Android
​
I would think that the next biggest selling point would actually be that the Hiby RS2 II is a dedicated local file playing, pure audio, digital audio player. Rather than some streaming player with all of the bells, whistles, and features as well as all of the auditory casualties that comes with an Android dap. This is a dap for the purist. It’s a dap for those who greatly appreciate music in its “potential” purest and cleanest form when considering a digital audio player. The RS2 II comes with no Bluetooth, no WiFi, no extra noise, no installing apps, no distractions. Just your local files, attach some iems, and then just enjoy your tunes while that beautiful screen presents your album art in full glorious view. To some this is the last thing that they would ever want. I perfectly understand those people too. There have been many moments during this review period where I wished I would’ve had the convenience of an Android dap. In truth, a handful of years ago I would’ve thought that you were out of your mind to go non-Android and give up so many features and ease of use convenience. Sure, the RS2 II isn’t for everyone, but I can tell you with absolute assurance that I find its special tone, timbre, and overall musicality infectious and that is all I truly care about. To add to that, there is something so nice about all those bells and whistles being gone. Somehow I am more connected to my music, to full albums, and I’m enjoying them in a different way. I can see why someone would consider a non-Android experience a true selling point. Especially a good device. 
Output Power
​
This is an area that I am very impressed by. So, Hiby went and about doubled the output power in the new RS2 II at 630 mW max power from the OG RS2 which has about 320 mW at max output. The RS2 II is supported by four analogue stage OPA1612 amp sections as well as four OPA1622 output amp devices. All things considered, the RS2 II is a little powerhouse for the size as it can give a fairly large total of 172.5 mW max output on 3.5 single ended as well. The bonus is that I don’t hear any audible hiss or noise with sensitive sets and I can drive any iem I could dream of very well. Now, even though it carries 630 mW of max output, it still can only drive efficient over-ear cans. Harder to drive sets can strain on the RS2 II a bit. So be advised. Granted, I drove the moderately efficient 
Sendy Audio Apollo Pro
 fairly well, with headroom to spare. However, the 
Sivga SV021 Pro
 was easy to drive. Certainly, some solid numbers that I know many of you will be happy to see. 
That Screen
​

I think that the screen used on the RS2 II is one of its best features. I only say that because first; it is very responsive. The touchscreen works perfectly, never lag, always fast. Next, the screen is stated as being 3.55” in size which is over an inch larger than the previous RS2 (2.45”). I also read that the RS2 II has a 480 x 360 display which gives it approximately 263 pixels per inch. Also, it is a very bright screen. Easy to see in sunlight. However, I like this screen best for how my album art appears. It’s always vibrant, very crisp and defined. Of course, in settings you have a bunch of touchscreen settings to choose from like double-tap to wake, adjustable font sizes, screen timeout controls, 180-degree screen rotation, as well as theme color choices. I know we are inundated with screens everywhere, but on a standalone music player having a well working and beautiful screen is a huge plus.
Sound Filters
​
One of the really great features on the Hiby RS2 II is that Hiby supplies many different sound filters. Sound Filters are different ways of reconstructing a digital signal prior to it becoming analogue. Basically, these filters preserve the most wanted audio information while attenuating or suppressing the unwanted high frequency info that is created during the conversion process. Of course, different filters are going to make different compromises and changes in this process. These filters do not make grand tonal changes or and are much closer to very fine adjustments. For some listeners who can discern and hear the changes at times these filters will notice that they can produce very subtle changes in the contour of note edges, transients, and also in the treble region. Remember, changing any region has an effect frequency wide. One may interpret these changes as softer, slightly crisper, more sharply defined, more relaxed, and even brighter. Now, with the RS2 II, Hiby provided many of these filters. I am simply going to name them off and may speak about them in my review. Also, these filters only work in OS mode or without using NOS. Keep that in mind. To begin, go into the Home page and touch the “Darwin” tab. Inside you’ll see 3 tabs. One labeled Digital Filter, one labeled NOS, and one labeled Harmonic Controller. Inside of the “Digital Filter” tab you’ll see Darwin Default, Linear Phase Sharp Roll-Off, Linear Phase Sharp Late Roll-Off, Linear Phase Short Ring, Linear Phase Short Ring Late Roll-Off, Minimum Phase Sharp Roll-Off, Minimum Phase Sharp Late Roll-Off, Minimum Phase Short Ring, Minimum Phase Short Ring Late Roll-Off, 0th Order Hold NOS, and Darwin Ultra. Go back to the three tabs and look at the NOS tab. It’s actually a button which activates or turns off NOS (Non-Oversampling). Under that is Harmonic Controller. Now, the Harmonic Controller is simply an adjustment for secondary harmonics from 0-255. 
NOS
​
I should quickly speak on the NOS tab because it actually does make an audible difference in how you hear the RS2 II. When NOS is activated it simply means that oversampling is bypassed. In my honest opinion, with NOS activated, the sound is closer to earthy organic and not as crisp as in the default OS mode. I found that there is a touch more warmth with NOS activated as well as a touch more low-end flavor into the mix. It’s actually the biggest change that I’ve heard from an NOS filter on any device. Definitely something to consider. Now, in OS mode you can then change any filter that I listed above. 
MSEB
​
Hiby offers a wide range of ways to dial in the sound to suit your preferences. Of course, this is a Hiby player, and all Hiby players can make use of the wonderfully popular MSEB functionality. The first I’ll quickly delve into is MSEB. One feature that is always worth noting within the Hiby Music ecosystem is the fantastically designed and imagined “MSEB”. If you don’t already know, MSEB is extremely popular and almost universally praised for how well designed it is. One of the easiest to understand and simplest EQ designs ever to hit the market. By the way, you can download Hiby Music on Android, and you’ll get this feature as well, just so you know. However, we are talking about the RS2 II at the moment. So, as you scroll through settings you will easily find the “Play Settings” in the Home Screen. Inside the Play Settings tab you can swap different filters, use PEQ, regular graphic EQ, among other things relevant to a digital audio player. You’ll also notice MSEB tuning which is a Hiby exclusive and does a fantastic job of tuning your music per your preferences. If you haven’t checked it out, then I would most certainly push you to do so. Again, MSEB is actually a type of equalizer which really helps to dial in the sound of any set to your own preferences. Actually, it’s about as easy as it gets. Hiby basically uses their own adjustable version of preset settings which are labeled and made ridiculously easy to learn and play around with. I don’t usually use any equalizer settings but for those who do, MSEB is a game changer. 
Conventional Graphic Equalizer
​
The Hiby RS2 II also offers a very easy to use 10-band graphic equalizer which works as any graphic EQ works. I found it cool that within the Hiby OS it allows me to change each frequency range up to +12 dbs or as little as -12 db’s, which is far greater than the standard 6-8 db’s on most graphic EQs. Honestly, it’s simple folks. Obviously, whatever you change can be saved as a profile for use whenever you’d like. It’s a nice feature. So many of you scream for flexibility and Hiby is giving you every conceivable way of doing that. Definitely cool to see. 
PEQ (Perimetric Equalizer) 
​
Another way of dialing in the sound to suit your constant need to change things up is a very well composed and simple to use Perimetric Equalizer (PEQ). The RS2 II provides up to 9-bands where you can easily decide or change the frequency, adjust Q, adjust the gain, decide if you want to use Low Shelf, Peaking, or High Shelf. It’s one of those PEQ’s that gives you every way of designing the tuning to fit your desires and it’s very fun to do. Just like MSEB and the Graphic EQ you can also save your profiles that you’ve created for use on this device. Now, I will say that there were some fat finger moments on the smaller screen, but I eventually figured out how to do everything efficiently and effectively. Once again, a dope feature, especially in this day and age. 
Battery Life
​
Another quality feature for such a small yet powerful device is the battery life. The total that Hiby states isn’t bad, though to some it may seem a bit low in comparison with other daps. Hiby declares that you can effectively get about 9.1 hours of battery life in 3.5 single ended listening as well as 8.1 hours using 4.4 balanced. Now, there are so many ways to skew that number but there are two definite ways to lessen those numbers. The first obviously being screen-on time. When the screen is on, the Backlight is on, the components running the screen are on, and the battery powers it. The longer you use it and brighter you use it will make a difference in how long your battery lasts. Next, if you listen with high gain, use 4.4 balanced, and listen to high-quality files you are going to lessen battery life. Coincidentally, I listen loud, I listen to all quality music files, and I’m always in high gain and almost always use the 4.4 balanced port. Oddly enough, I still feel that I am getting around 7 hours of battery life. Really folks. I almost wonder if Hiby downplayed the max hours. They’ve had some criticism in the past with the R6 Pro II and a couple others as battery life wasn’t exceptional. Not bad, but not super great. Honestly, folks, for an R2R Dac with Darwin III tech running the show and such a powerful little device, getting as many hours as I’m getting is a huge bonus. Most certainly a “Pro” for me. 
Dual Micro SD Slots
​
I find this to be one of the most useful and most awesome features that Hiby could’ve added and you only understand how good it is when you need it. I adore this feature. Like daps of old Hiby decided to give the Hiby RS2 II two different SD-Card slots. The beautiful thing is that each one can give you up to 2 tb of storage. So many of these daps nowadays only provide one SD card slot, but having two means that I can grow my library very-very large without much worry of running out of space on the RS2 II. 
Indexing Limit
​
Because I know I will get asked this question, I do not know if Hiby put an indexing limit for total number of indexed tracks on the Hiby RS2 II. I can tell you that I have about 900 GB of music on this device which probably works out to around 30,000-38,000 tracks. I have not seen any indication that there has been any limit, at all. I can try to find out and edit the answer into this section. However, Hiby added two micro-SD card slots and both slots provide 2 tb each of potential storage capacity. It would be very strange for Hiby to provide that sort of potential to only cap the amount of indexed tracks that could be added. Okay, moving on.
Sound Impressions
​
*
Note
: before I dive into my sound impressions of the Hiby RS2 II, I first want to speak on a few things. First off, I did not burn-in the RS2 II. I did complete many hours of listening-in. I do not feel that any major changes occurred. This device sounded good on day one and still sounds very good today. Next, I used many different iems and headphones for critical listening, far too many to list off here. I listen to flac or better files which are stored on my SD card inside of the RS2 II. Also, my impressions below come from the factory settings. I do switch between NOS and other filters from time to time, but I will explain that in my review.
​
Source Reviews
​
Ialways feel it’s at least somewhat necessary to explain my thoughts on a source review when it comes to sound. I believe that the bulk of what you hear, the flavor, timbre, tonality, all mostly comes from the transducer (iem or headphones). All the source can do is further tailor the sound that the transducer has created, which is no small thing. In fact, oftentimes I have found that it’s the source which truly adds the final shaping of sound and brings my listening session over-the-top. A source can slightly offer a hint of warmth, some coolness, some brilliance, more clarity, it can slightly enrich or slightly thin/dry a note. I always say that sources more-so nudge the sound, they help shape the sound to an extent. However, I think it’s better said that a source doesn’t reshape the voice of an iem, it edges it, it can add subtle contour, help the decadent flow, and a good source will give the iem the electrical conditions (so to speak) to speak clearly. That said, it is always the transducer which does the true legwork and has the most say in how the sound will come across. I say all of this because you’ll read words like “influence”, “persuade”, “invoke”, etc. which is how I feel a source can really make its contribution felt. I’m not getting into the how. That goes into output impedance, output voltage, power, noise floor, distortion, and many other variables which help a good source to make a difference. I think at the end of the day it’s the iem/headphones which do the auditory heavy lifting. The iem is the paint on the brush, but the source is the canvas that the brush paints on. Both are very important for the end result. Good pairing is important, good matching from source to transducer, but I can tell you that there’s been many times that finding the right source was the reason my listening session went from good… to great.
What’s It Sound Like? 
​

The Hiby RS2 II embodies a more musical and engaging flavor, and if you ask me, that’s exactly what should make it a sought after source device. The type of sound character that always influences an organic sweetness to just about any set of iems or headphones that I attach to it. Musicality-First, immersive, and highly proficient at drawing out the emotional sentiment in a track better than most daps in its range. However, it is well capable of presenting details when it needs to as well. It just isn’t the type of dap that pushes those details at the listener and it isn’t one that boosts presence brilliance to illuminate those details. The best way to tell you is that the RS2 II is musically enhanced and fluid with a slightly relaxed tilt, without losing any clarity, and without influencing a 
less-clean
 sound for my iems/headphones. Relaxed and clean are not opposites (though it seems they should be) and they can easily exist together, the RS2 II proves that. Now, the RS2 II is not some razor-sharp, detail tracking, analytically tuned device. Yes, it is very clean and doesn’t add audible hiss or noise, and yes, the RS2 II will draw out subtle details very well, but it will always provide a sense of engagement first. Engagement is the mission for this dap and any technical acuity is just icing on the cake. It carries a very flavorful sound that will never add dryness, and it will always bolster a more robust note body. The RS2 II is not quite 
earthy-organic
 in its timbre, and it’s also not what I’d call 
analogue 
either. Instead, clean-organic is the best way for me to describe it. The thing that grabbed me right away was the dimensional sound field influence on my iems and how the tone-flow and cadence always persuades a smoother portrayal of my music, which is utterly and completely engaging. For me, personally, I always tend to feel that emotionality within music is more apparent with a slightly warmer and less sharp sound and this is exactly true based on my experience with the RS2 II. There is something so enticing and satisfying about a device this compact providing such an engrossing feel to my music. I mean, in comparison to some other daps in its price point.Such a cool yet serious little pocket player! I’d also say that the timbre influence provided by the RS2 II always nudges my iems/headphones to a slightly more organic character. 
Relaxed? 
​

I’d also say that the RS2 II carries a slightly less exciting presence about it. It will not add loads of dynamic energy or tonal contrast and will not add tons of extra vibrancetto your iems. Not in an immediate and energetic sense anyway. What it does is “retain” tonal contrast and dynamic presence in its own organic way, rather than add it. Granted, it is also not so smoothly rendered and earthy that it sands-down fine edges on notes or kills the clinical precision of an analytical sounding iem. Like listening with the 
Simgot EA1000
. A set that is bright, dynamic, big macro-dynamics, highly detailed. A set that’s highly recommended and beloved for its technical acuity and for its energetic sound. However, the RS2 II does a good job of harnessing that energy with a slightly more measured amount of radiant effulgence, toning it down a tad, helping the EA1000 to come across more controlled, less abrasive, while not losing its clean-lined note definition. That is so very important. In fact, I find the RS2 II to be a perfect complement to the EA1000 tuning. Especially with NOS activated (which adds a touch of warmth). I actually hesitate to call the RS2 II “relaxed” because I don’t want you getting the impression that it offers slower transients, or that it will blunt your analytical iems/headphones. The RS2 II doesn’t do that. It has this pervasive rhythm-based demeanor, but that rhythmicity remains clean, open, and transparent. To add to that, in my opinion, the RS2 II retains textured note surfaces, and it retains the tight transient attack of a more vivacious and speedy set. What I love is that it won’t enhance or exaggerate aggressive peaks, and it won’t promote glare, ever. So, while I call the RS2 II “relaxed”, please understand that I’m not saying that the RS2 II has any less technical chops when it needs to. Surely, it won’t be as technically on-point as some super sharp ESS Sabre or Cirrus Logic daps. But it always maintains a clean canvas for my iems, it doesn’t add veil, and the RS2 II always seems to promote cleanly rendered note-to-note dexterity. Again, it simply won’t “add” energy and the RS2 II won’t force brilliance upon the transducer, nor will it muddy the mix of a warmer set. It’s quite wonderful for the cost. 
Timbre & Tone Color
​
If I were to describe its tonal coloration, I’d say the Hiby RS2 II sounds closest to warm-neutral. Like, neutrality with a dose of gentle warmth. I’d never call the sound influence as lush, or even warm-rich, and definitely not dark. It’s not so rolled-off up top or low-end enhanced to call it any of those descriptors. Again, it retains tonal contrast of any iem that I attach to it as it lets most iems/headphones be what they were tuned to be without totally changing tonal influence. Timbre is natural and cohesive, semi-rich, and always promotes a note body that is more robust, rather than sprightly and thin, good note density. All of my sets retain their transient speed; they retain an unsullied sound (if they are tuned this way) and they retain an analytical tilt (depending on the set). On the flipside, a warmer and thicker sounding set like the 
Letshuoer Ember
, which carries a warm and rich sound doesn’t all of a sudden sound veiled or muddy attached to the RS2 II. Actually, the Ember sounds more open, it sounds bodied, it sounds very engaging, but that gentle warmth of the RS2 II doesn’t exaggerate the warmth of the Ember. The same can be said of the 
Aful Explorer
 or any other warm-tilted iem. Okay, now that I’ve spoken at length of its tonal character (to exhaustion) and repeated myself over and over again trying to explain this device, why don’t we quickly run through each 3rd of the mix… 
Ooh, such a sweet pairing. The ODA Leviathan T800 & the RS2 II are so good
​
Bass Region
​

To me the bass has a moderately authoritative quality to it listening with the factory settings. There is a presence added to the region from some other daps. I’d call the bass warm and expansive with solid enough note control. In my opinion it actually better controlled than the previous RS2’s looser bass tuning. I would not call the bass region overly “boosted” or “enhanced” but it is substantial enough to promote musical scale over fine-tuned precision or definition. Certainly not some highly textured bass influence. I’d more-so liken the RS2 II’s bass region as a strong foundation beneath the music rather than bass enhanced. Essentially, the RS2 II carries a full-bodied sound down low and probably a less sharp attack than other daps, but very engaging too. More of a substance and atmosphere type of persuasion, rather than a super sharp attack that helps display every last textured detail. This bass plays right into the overall sonic theme of the RS2 II. That is, musicality-first, engagement-first, emotionally charged and highly immersive. It’s all about tone-flow, macro-clarity, and rhythmic smoothness in its cleanest form. I actually adore the low-end on the RS2 II because it doesn’t push any sort of veil across the mix and never adds mudd. It’s a clean low-end for the tuning, perhaps a hair softer in attack, but highly addictive in timbre, tonality, and atmosphere within my music. There’s an uptick in bass note density as well from other daps. I’m not saying it’ll turn the Aful Explorer into a bass canon either. What I’m talking about is note density, note fullness, rigidity, and haptic feel, as each note has a compacted and firm influence on my iems. It’s what I would call “high quality atmospheric”. Absolutely engrossing. The RS2 II still retains nice note definition for its style along with a very agile start and stop dexterity. So, to condense all of my bass thoughts. The Hiby RS2 II’s bass has nice presence and offers a foundational style bass, more about substance than fine-lined texture. Yet dense, clean, and robust with solid note-to-note nimbleness. The RS2 II doesn’t have the sharpest and most hard-lined attack, but it’s defined well enough and does a wonderful job of adding an immersive feel to my music. I love it. 
Midrange
​
Now, the midrange performance on the Hiby RS2 II is what I personally love the most. I find that the mids always provide a full-bodied and smooth presentation, enhancing engagement and always influencing a more organic timbre to any iem/headphones that I attach to this dap. The bonus is that I also hear a boost in sound field dimensionality that really plays into the overall immersion into my music. The mids are slightly warmed against a mostly neutral tonal coloration with a pleasing sense of substance to every note. I’d probably say the mids are somewhat forward and emboldened, which plays right into some of the nicest vocals (depending on the iem/headphones) that I’ve had the pleasure of hearing under $700. Friends, please hear me. If you have the 
Letshuoer Mystic 8
 (thank for the recommendation Fahim) on hand, the 
EPZ 550
, the 
Twistura WoodNote
, 
Sivga Lyrebird
, and any other iem with a propensity for good vocals then you will see just how well the RS2 II’s midrange fills-out vocal inflections and embosses male and female voices. It’s utterly addicting folks. Not just voices either. Lead instruments have body without bloat, they’re crisp when a track calls for crispness, there’s zero added veil, and damn near all iems/headphones have good note intelligibility on the RS2 II. They’re also well defined, resolute, and clean, with just enough texture and vibrant sparkle. However, that resolution, definition, and cleanliness aren’t created from boosted brilliance, but rather quality components, clean background, no noise, and an open sound field that promotes better separation & clarity. Even if it’s more organic in timbre. Definitely not resolving or clean in an analytical way. This is the beauty of the RS2 II. I love that the RS2 II never diminishes the vibrant shimmer within the midrange of my iems either. It simply will not exaggerate that brilliance and vibrance into glare or shout. If that makes sense? 
Midrange Cont…
​

I will say that listening in NOS mode most certainly provides a slightly thicker and more earthy timbre to my music. Stuff like lower midrange male vocals come through a touch more bodied, less resolved, and oddly enough just as engaging. Furthermore, females and upper midrange lead instrumentation doesn’t have quite the same tinsley sparkle and crispness. However, it doesn’t matter what filter you are using because the RS2 II’s midrange always exhibits the same organic, clean, and forward flavor. Just, slightly different in note density and slight differences in texture around the edges of notes. Now, in the factory settings I was almost taken aback as I really didn’t expect such a well-done technical experience. Like I said earlier, sound separation is great, resolution is better than expected, and the sound field does feel more realistic than some other daps. However, if I am using an analytical iem like the 
Sivga Que UTG
, or even a kilo-buck 
Letshuoer Cadenza 12
, it is utter awesome how well the RS2 II can filter those subtle details to the surface, cleanly partition off elements within the sound field, as well as cleanly place instruments as well. Don’t mistake my words though. The RS2 II is not some highly technical detail beast of a dap. I have solid technically-based daps and they clearly are more clinical. Of course, the timbre trade-offs are too great. Hence why I greatly enjoy the RS2 II. Hiby did a wonderful job. 
Treble Region
​

This brings us to the treble which is one of smooth in & out tone flow, moderately emphasized, and is all about natural integration into the mix rather than sharp distinctness. It’s the type of treble that will uphold a solid treble iem and draw details forward if a set presents the spectrum in that manner. However, it is also the type of treble that will always promote musicality first, engagement first, and is much more of a cohesive partner to the rest of the mix then anything else. I’d also say that the RS2 II’s treble is not a bright treble. In fact, it has what I’d call reasonable brilliance. Enough to create a balance without ever calling attention to the region. The timbre is natural, note body is generally natural too, where high-frequency elements and sounds seem to keep a fluid connection to the body of an instrument sounding rhythmically homogenized rather than sounding like a dry, laser etched, or detached layer within that brilliance. It’s all about cohesiveness folks. That’s what the entire tuning is about. The treble simply walks that line. Just like the bass, just like the mids. I hear very nice note separation and macro clarity, yet without it sounding analytically precise or dry, which is great. Also, a bright iem will sound more palatable without losing its character, while a darker treble iem will come across with better note contours yet zero “added” brightness. That is an important distinction. The RS2 II treble isn’t trying to change what a set is. That said, for some folks there may be a slight lack of extra crispness & sharpness I suppose (especially with NOS enabled). Granted, I am rarely actually listening for “crispness” unless I am going down my review checklist and purposefully zeroing in on such a thing. So I honestly don’t feel that it is a problem. Altogether, it’s a clean and organic treble that keeps an even keel. It won’t add harshness, it’s smoother in cadence, and it upholds the overall tuning of this R2R dap very well. 
Technicalities
​

I think I’ve pretty much answered this question but I suppose I’ll do my due diligence and repeat myself. So, the Hiby RS2 II was absolutely not tuned to be some technically inclined wonder machine built for extraction of details, dry and clinical excavation of subtle and minute minutia, and it simply was not tuned with artificially boosted luminance. Every good technical trait on the RS2 II comes from the use of quality components and a smart tuning. I hear what I would call “preserved & organically retained details”. Of course the RS2 II also carries solid micro details with sets (iems/headphones) that are tuned to draw out details. However, the RS2 II will not turn a warm, rich, smooth, bassy, and musically gifted set into a detail tracker. That will never happen. Let’s put it this way; the Hiby RS2 II is solid technically for what it is. That is; a highly musical, smoothly rendered, enthralling, emotion capturing, and totally engaging dap. Now, I definitely find that note separation is above average, imaging is extremely well laid out, and I certainly hear good sound field dimensionality. Now, I wouldn’t exactly say the RS2 II provides my sets some wide and vast stage. Of course, most of what you hear when it comes to stage size and vastness comes from the transducer. Still, it seems to help most sets with better spaciousness and very solid scalability, depth of field, even nice height to the stage. In fact, one of the 1st things that I noticed when listening to the 
Simgot SuperMix 5
 was how dimensionally well established that set sounds. I’d say holographic. I hear clean layers front to back, solid vertical layering. It gets even better using better iems like the 
ODA Leviathan T800
 which sounds effortlessly technical while only coming across even more robust in note weight and of course remaining highly tuneful. The best quality of the RS2 II is that it is always melodic and harmonious and does so in a clean manner. Again, don’t expect the most highly technical dap, but do expect an engaging and immersive listen. 
Last Words on the Hiby RS2 II 
​
It took me all of 2 minutes to decide that I loved this dap. Friends, my favorite dap under $1k is easily the Shanling M6 Ultra. Even though it is almost 4 years old it is still the best sounding dap that I’ve heard. I cannot tell you how close the RS2 II gets to the M6 Ultra, but it’s so close that it’s scary. It’s also $350-400 less in cost. Of course, the RS2 II doesn’t have all the bells and whistles and isn’t some super feature rich player. The RS2 II is exactly what it was promoted to be; a standalone R2R music player that was crafted and created solely for listening to local files on SD-cards. It is exactly that and it does so extremely well. I didn’t gloat nearly enough about the sound quality within my review because I don’t want to push my praise into hype, but I am so greatly impressed with what Hiby has created that it has literally become the number one source that I reach for of late. Which speaks volumes. I am not patting myself on the back or bragging, but I have many sources after all of these years reviewing. The RS2 II offers one of the most gratifying playback abilities of almost all of them. Once again, it costs $439! Because of that, they can keep the bells and whistles, I don’t need them. They can keep the wifi, the Bluetooth, the apps, I don’t need them. I get all of the satisfaction that I need out of the RS2 II from simply tapping the play button on the touchscreen or clicking the button on the side. Absolutely awesome job Hiby! 
Not For Everyone 
​

However, as with anything in this hobby the RS2 II is not going to be for everyone. That’s just the plain and simple truth. In fact I’d say that audio purists who simply want a dap that can play their high-res files are the vast minority anymore. Now, I do think people are coming around, but they are certainly in the minority. However, the largest reason that the RS2 II will be quickly overlooked and forgotten is because it has no ability to stream music. How many people in this hobby stream their music? I can answer that for you… a lot! There are clear limitations to the RS2 II which will keep it from being purchased. Not everyone has a built up local library of music and albums like I and others have. So again, there are definitely good reasons that some folks will not purchase the RS2 II. To many it will be a huge problem that the RS2 II doesn’t have any wifi ability or any Bluetooth ability. Not having Bluetooth also means that you don’t have Hiby Link, which I use all the time on daps like the Hiby R3 Pro II, or other smaller daps. Hiby Link would have been very nice. You cannot load different apps, and you are stuck with the Hiby OS. Of course, I personally like how Hiby laid-out Hiby OS on the RS2 II, but I can’t do anything but listen to files on this device. Also, as far as listening, not everyone wants a more relaxed sound. Some folks want edge, excitement, and overt vibrance and they won’t necessarily get that to the degree that they may like on the RS2 II. It won’t have the super finely textured note surfaces as some would like and it flat-out just won’t be an analytically tuned dap. It has other little quirks like slightly less battery life than the original and it cannot drive demanding headphones perfectly either. Still, if you ask me the Hiby RS2 II is a sensational dap and I’m very glad to have it in my collection. Also, that $439 price is well worth the cost in my opinion. The RS2 II is an easy recommendation from me.
